entries.title: types
entries.summary: Integer and floating-point types, sizes, and how values are converted.
entries.syntax: int8_t … int64_t, uint8_t … uint64_t, size_t, char, short, int, long, float, double, void, bool
entries.description:
Use the fixed-width types of <stdint.h> when the size matters (`int32_t`, `uint8_t`). `size_t` is the unsigned type of `sizeof` and of most sizes and counts in the library; print it with `%zu`. `char` is for text; for a raw byte use `uint8_t`. `bool`, `true` and `false` need <stdbool.h> (C99); before that, 0 is false and any other value is true.
In an expression the narrower operand is promoted to the wider type; in an assignment the value is converted to the type of the variable (floating point → integer truncates toward zero). A cast `(type) expr` forces a conversion.

details.name: integer division
details.text: `7 / 2` is 3 and `-7 / 2` is -3 (truncation toward zero); `7 % 2` is 1.

details.name: mixed arithmetic
details.text: `7 / 2.0` is 3.5. `(double) a / b` converts before dividing; `(double)(a / b)` converts after.

details.name: float literals
details.text: `3.14` is a double, `3.14f` a float; `10L` is a long.

mistakes: Dividing two ints and expecting a fraction.
Assuming `int` or `long` has a given size.

entries.title: limits.h
entries.summary: Minimum and maximum values of the integer types.
entries.description: The constants tell you the range of each type on the current system. On Linux x86-64: `CHAR_BIT` 8, `INT_MAX` 2147483647, `LONG_MAX` 9223372036854775807. Going beyond the range of a signed type is undefined behaviour; unsigned types wrap around.
entries.example:
#include <limits.h>
printf("%d\n", INT_MAX);   /* 2147483647 */
mistakes: Signed overflow: `INT_MAX + 1` is undefined.

entries.title: operators
entries.summary: Arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise and assignment operators, with precedence.
entries.description: Precedence from highest to lowest: `()` `[]` `.` `->`; unary `! ~ ++ -- + - * & sizeof (cast)` (right to left); `* / %`; `+ -`; `<< >>`; `< <= > >=`; `== !=`; `&`; `^`; `|`; `&&`; `||`; `?:`; assignments (right to left); `,`. When in doubt, add parentheses.

details.text: logical operators, yielding 0 or 1. `&&` and `||` short-circuit: the right side is evaluated only if needed (`p != NULL && p->x > 0` is safe).
`i++` yields the old value then increments; `++i` increments first.
bitwise and, or, xor, not on every bit
shift left / right: `x << n` multiplies by 2^n
`c ? a : b` is `a` when `c` is true, else `b`

details.name: % (modulo)
details.text: remainder of the integer division; the sign follows the dividend

mistakes: Writing `=` instead of `==` in a condition.
Modifying the same variable twice in one expression (`i = i++ + 1`): undefined.

entries.title: if
entries.summary: Run code only when a condition is true (else: otherwise).
entries.description: The condition is an integer: 0 is false, anything else is true. Braces are optional around a single statement but always safer. `else` pairs with the nearest `if`.
mistakes: A stray `;` after `if (…)` makes the body empty.
Comparing floats with `==`.

entries.title: switch
entries.summary: Choose between several integer values.
entries.syntax: switch (expr) { case v1: …; break; case v2: …; break; default: …; }
entries.description: `expr` must be an integer (char included); each `case` needs a constant. Execution continues into the next `case` until a `break` (fall-through), which is occasionally useful and often a bug. `default` handles every other value.
mistakes: Forgetting `break`.
Using strings or floats as `case` values (not allowed).

entries.title: while
entries.summary: Repeat while a condition is true (checked before each pass).
entries.description: The body runs zero or more times. Something inside must eventually make the condition false (or use `break`).
mistakes: Forgetting to update the variable: infinite loop.

entries.title: do
entries.summary: do … while: repeat, checking the condition after each pass (at least one pass).
entries.description: Useful when the body must run once before the test, such as asking for a value until it is valid. Note the `;` after the condition.
mistakes: Forgetting the final `;`.

entries.title: for
entries.summary: Counting loop: initialise; test; update.
entries.description: `init` runs once, `cond` is tested before every pass and `update` runs after every pass. All three parts are optional (`for (;;)` is an infinite loop). A variable declared in `init` (C99) exists only inside the loop.
entries.example:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    sum += v[i];
mistakes: Off-by-one: `<=` instead of `<` when walking an array.
A stray `;` after the `)` makes the body empty.

entries.title: break
entries.summary: Leave the innermost loop or switch immediately.
entries.description: Control continues after the loop or switch. It does not leave outer loops.

entries.title: continue
entries.summary: Skip the rest of this loop pass and start the next.
entries.description: In a `for` loop the update expression still runs before the next test.

entries.title: return
entries.summary: Leave the current function, optionally giving back a value.
entries.description: In `main`, the value is the exit status of the program (0 = success). A function must not return the address of one of its local variables.
mistakes: Returning a pointer to a local array.

entries.title: functions
entries.summary: Declaring (prototype) and defining functions; arguments are passed by value.
entries.syntax:
type name(type a, type b);   /* prototype */
type name(type a, type b) { … return value; }
entries.description: A function must be declared before it is called, at least by a prototype. Arguments are copies: to let a function change the caller's variable, pass its address and write through the pointer. An array argument is passed as a pointer to its first element, so pass the length separately. `void` in the return type means no value; `f(void)` means no parameters.
mistakes: Writing `swap(int a, int b)` and expecting the caller's variables to change.
Using a function before declaring it.

entries.title: main
entries.summary: The entry point; command-line arguments and environment.
entries.syntax:
int main(void)
int main(int argc, char *argv[])
int main(int argc, char *argv[], char *envp[])
entries.description: `argc` is the number of arguments including the program name; `argv[0]` is the program name and `argv[argc]` is NULL. Every argument is a string: use `atoi` or `strtol` for numbers. `envp` (a common Unix extension) is a NULL-terminated array of `NAME=value` strings; `getenv` is the portable way to read one. The value returned (or passed to `exit`) is the exit status: 0 means success.
mistakes: Starting at `argv[0]` and treating the program name as an argument.
Reading `argv[1]` without checking `argc`.

entries.title: static
entries.summary: Keep a local variable's value between calls, or make a global private to its file.
entries.description: Inside a function, a `static` variable is created once, initialised once (with a constant) and keeps its value between calls. At file level, `static` limits a variable or function to that source file.
mistakes: Expecting a static local to be re-initialised on each call.

entries.title: const
entries.summary: Declare a value that must not be changed.
entries.syntax: const type name = value;   const char *p;
entries.description: The compiler rejects assignments to a `const` object. `const char *p` is a pointer to characters you may not modify through `p`; library functions use it for parameters they only read. A `const` variable is a typed alternative to `#define` constants.
entries.example:
const int MAX = 64;
size_t strlen(const char *s);
mistakes: Casting `const` away and modifying a string literal.

entries.title: enum
entries.summary: Named integer constants.
entries.description: Values count up from 0 unless set (`C` above is 6). An enum type is an integer: it can be used in `switch` and compared. `typedef` gives it a shorter name.
entries.example:
enum color { RED, GREEN, BLUE };
enum color c = GREEN;   /* 1 */

entries.title: typedef
entries.summary: Give an existing type another name.
entries.description: Most often used to avoid writing `struct` every time, or to name an enum.

entries.title: struct
entries.summary: A record: several named members in one object.
entries.syntax: struct tag { type a; type b; };   struct tag v;   v.a   p->a
entries.description: Access members with `.` on a struct and `->` on a pointer to a struct (`p->x` is `(*p).x`). Assigning a struct copies all its members; structs can be passed to and returned from functions by value (large ones are usually passed by pointer). Initialise with `{1, 2}` or, in C99, `{.x = 1, .y = 2}`. `sizeof` may include padding.
mistakes: Writing `p.x` when `p` is a pointer.
Comparing two structs with `==` (not allowed).

entries.title: sizeof
entries.summary: Size in bytes of a type or object, as a size_t.
entries.description: Computed at compile time. On an array variable it is the size of the whole array; on a pointer it is the size of an address (4 or 8 bytes). When an array is passed to a function it becomes a pointer, so `sizeof` inside the function gives the pointer size.
mistakes: Using sizeof on a pointer parameter to count elements.

entries.title: pointers
entries.summary: Addresses: &, *, pointer arithmetic, NULL and void *.
entries.syntax: type *p;   p = &x;   *p = value;   p + 1   NULL   void *
entries.description: `&x` is the address of `x`; `*p` is the object `p` points to. `NULL` points to nothing and must not be dereferenced. Arithmetic is scaled by the pointed-to type: `p + 1` is `sizeof(*p)` bytes further. `a[i]` is `*(a + i)`. `void *` is a generic pointer that converts to and from any object pointer. Pointers are passed by value too: a function that must change the caller's pointer needs a `type **`.

details.name: p - q
details.text: number of elements between two pointers into the same array (a ptrdiff_t)

mistakes: Dereferencing NULL or an uninitialised pointer.
Keeping a pointer to an object that no longer exists (dangling pointer).

entries.title: arrays
entries.summary: Fixed-size sequences of elements of one type.
entries.syntax: type a[N];   type a[] = {…};   type m[R][C];
entries.description: Indices run from 0 to N-1 and are NOT checked: going outside is undefined behaviour. In most expressions the array name becomes a pointer to its first element. A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays, stored row after row. An array parameter is really a pointer, so the length must be passed too. `sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])` gives the element count of the real array.
mistakes: `v[5]` on a 5-element array (one past the end).
Reading an array that was never initialised.

entries.title: strings
entries.summary: A string is a char array ended by '\0'.
entries.description: There is no string type. A string of length n needs n + 1 bytes: the last one is the terminator `'\0'`. A literal like `"Hola"` lives in read-only memory: do not modify it through a `char *`; use an array for a modifiable copy. Compare contents with `strcmp`, never with `==` (that compares addresses). `<string.h>` has the functions.
mistakes: Allocating `strlen(s)` bytes instead of `strlen(s) + 1`.
`if (s == "yes")` compares pointers, not text.

entries.title: escapes
entries.summary: Escape sequences inside character and string literals.
entries.description: A backslash starts a special character. A string literal ends with an implicit `'\0'`. `'a'` is a char (an int in C) and `"a"` is a string of two bytes.

details.text: the null character that ends strings

details.name: \xhh \ooo
details.text: a character by hexadecimal or octal code

entries.example: printf("a\tb\n");   /* a, a tab, b, a newline */
mistakes: Writing `"\n"` where you meant the two characters backslash and n: use `"\\n"`.

entries.title: #include
entries.summary: Insert another file's text before compiling.
entries.description: `<…>` searches the system directories, `"…"` searches the current directory first (use it for your own headers). Headers contain declarations (prototypes, types, constants); the code of the library comes in at link time.
entries.example:
#include <stdio.h>    /* printf, fopen … */
#include "util.h"     /* your own header */
mistakes: Forgetting a header: the compiler then guesses the prototype (-Wall warns).

entries.title: #define
entries.summary: Define a text-substitution macro or a constant.
entries.description: The preprocessor replaces every use of the name by the text before compilation. Parenthesise macro parameters and the whole expansion. A `;` at the end of a `#define` becomes part of every expansion.
entries.example:
#define MAX_SIZE 64
#define SQR(x) ((x) * (x))
int v[MAX_SIZE];
int s = SQR(2 + 1);   /* 9, thanks to the parentheses */
mistakes: `#define SQR(x) x * x` makes `SQR(2 + 1)` expand to `2 + 1 * 2 + 1`.

entries.title: #ifdef
entries.summary: Conditional compilation and include guards.
entries.description: Code between the directives is compiled only if the condition holds. The classic include guard `#ifndef FILE_H` / `#define FILE_H` / … / `#endif`, or `#pragma once`, keeps a header from being included twice.
entries.example:
#ifndef UTIL_H
#define UTIL_H
int media(int a, int b);
#endif
